Taiwanese inventors tended to focus on applying new technologies to develop practical solutions that could make everyday life easier for people, Ghafooripour said.
Nearly every Taiwanese team won an award, and the gold medal count was the highest for Taiwan since it first participated in the Silicon Valley International Inventions Festival in 2018.

title: How a personalised cancer vaccine could cut risk of death by half
content:
5 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Aug 23, 2026 03:18 PM IST

A new personalised cancer vaccine, administered along with a popular immunotherapy drug Keytruda, has been shown to reduce the risk of death owing to recurrence and spread of skin cancer. Developed by pharmaceutical giant Merck and the mRNA vaccine company Moderna, intismeran is the first such therapy to show meaningful clinical benefits.
“These Phase 3 findings represent a pivotal moment for the field of cancer research. For many years, the idea of creating an mRNA treatment designed specifically for an individual patient’s cancer was aspirational. We are now helping turn that vision into a reality,” said Stéphane Bancel, CEO of Moderna, in a press release.
Here’s how the vaccine would work, what the Merck-Moderna study found, and its significance for cancer treatment in India.
Story continues below this ad



How does intismeran work?
The therapy is designed by identifying the mutations in a patient’s tumour sample: together, these identifying proteins — called neoantigens — act like the fingerprint of their cancer. Neoantigens are essentially proteins that are found only on the cancerous cells, which the body’s immune system can be trained to recognise. These neoantigens vary from person to person, meaning they become an identifier for their cancer but also necessitating personalised vaccines.
The vaccine consists of synthetically developed mRNA that encodes for these proteins. mRNA, or messenger RNA, is a single-stranded molecule that carries genetic instructions from DNA in the cell nucleus. By telling the cell which proteins to make, it acts as a molecular blueprint. Each treatment consists of mRNA coding for 34 such neoantigens. Once administered, the body generates these proteins and presents them to the immune system.
The idea behind the therapy is the same as any other vaccine: teach the immune system to recognise the cancer’s fingerprint so that it can mount an effective response whenever it spots these mutated cells.
“Just as a vaccine for an infectious disease contains the antigen from a pathogen —  the proteins or lipids that trains the body’s immune system to recognise and fight off the pathogen — therapies such as this contain cancer neoantigens. While people have been working on this for a decade or so, this is the first clinical breakthrough,” Dr Gaurav Kharya, haematologist and co-founder of the startup developing blood cancer treatment Cellogen, told The Indian Express.
Story continues below this ad
“The benefit is that this fingerprint of the cancer goes into the immune system’s memory. So, if the cancer comes back, the body’s immune system can immediately recognise it and mount a response, prolonging recurrence-free survival,” he added.
What did the study find?
The study found that when the vaccine was given with the popular immunotherapy drug Keytruda, the risk of death owing to recurrence of skin cancer went down by 49% — and the risk of death owing to its spreading went down by 59%.
The results are in comparison to only Keytruda being used, which in itself has over the years shown to be much more effective in treatment of certain cancers as compared to traditional chemotherapy.
The most common side effects noted in the study were fatigue, injection site pain, and chills.
Is this significant for India?
Story continues below this ad
When it comes to the current treatment, the impact would be limited, say oncologists. This is mainly because of two reasons:
One, the current trial result is only meant for skin cancer, or melanoma. “While melanoma is one of the most common types of cancer in the caucasian population, it is not commonly seen among Indians. Melanoma is, in fact, rare here,” Dr Abhishek Shankar, oncologist at AIIMS-New Delhi, told The Indian Express. Globocan — short for Global Cancer Observatory, an online platform that maintains global cancer statistics — shows that melanoma accounts for only 0.26% of all cancer cases in India and 0.17% of deaths.
Two, is the cost factor. While Keytruda has been shown to be effective in the treatment of several types of cancers, most patients in India are unable to afford it, even with patient assistance programmes.
A real-world study from Tata Memorial Hospital had shown that only 1.6% of the patients who need such immunotherapy are able to access them. “Cost is a very significant factor in India. How can they afford the combination therapy when they cannot afford the immunotherapy itself?” said Shankar.

title: Pritzker firma una nueva ley para conductores de Uber y Lyft en Illinois: qué podrán negociar con las aplicaciones
content:
Pritzker firma una nueva ley para conductores de Uber y Lyft en Illinois: qué podrán negociar con las aplicaciones
Ahora los trabajadores podrán abordar sus compensaciones económicas de manera directa con las empresas de transporte
- 3 minutos de lectura'
El gobernador de Illinois, JB Pritzker, firmó una legislación que otorga derechos de negociación colectiva a más de 100 mil conductores de vehículos compartidos. Esta normativa implica un cambio importante en las condiciones de trabajo dentro de la economía de plataformas digitales, como Uber y Lyft.
Qué podrán negociar los conductores de Uber y Lyft bajo la nueva ley de Illinois
Pritzker firmó la Ley de Relaciones Laborales de Conductores de Redes de Transporte el 7 de agosto de 2026, que entró en vigor de inmediato. Esta legislación establece un marco estatal definitivo que permite a los trabajadores de plataformas digitales agruparse en organizaciones laborales.
Según el texto legal de la medida, la nueva normativa faculta a los representantes de los conductores para negociar de manera directa con las empresas de transporte. Entre las materias que deberán abordarse en la negociación se encuentran:
- Compensación económica y tarifas base por cada viaje realizado.
- Beneficios y coberturas por accidentes o lesiones laborales.
- Medidas y protocolos de seguridad para los conductores.
- Licencia pagada por enfermedad o emergencias familiares.
- Procedimientos y apelaciones vinculados con la desactivación de cuentas.
- Otras condiciones de trabajo que afecten directamente su sustento.
Los promotores de la iniciativa celebraron esta legislación como un triunfo histórico para el sector laboral de la región. El proyecto de ley recibió un fuerte apoyo por parte de la unión de conductores y diversos activistas sindicales.
Uber y Lyft en Illinois: qué cambia con la negociación colectiva de los conductores
Las corporaciones como Uber y Lyft enfrentan ahora un escenario de regulación que transforma su modelo de negocio tradicional en el estado. Las empresas deberán reconocer a los representantes elegidos por los conductores para entablar las mesas de negociación obligatorias.
La ley obliga a negociar la compensación de los conductores, aunque las plataformas mantienen el control sobre sus precios y las políticas de desactivación. Asimismo, la ley prohíbe que las compañías trasladen los nuevos costos operativos directamente a las tarifas que pagan los usuarios finales.
La medida busca un equilibrio entre el desarrollo de la innovación tecnológica y el respeto a los derechos laborales de los trabajadores. La administración estatal vigilará que las plataformas cumplan con las disposiciones de la nueva estructura legal.
Cuánto pagarán Uber y Lyft por viaje para financiar el nuevo sistema en Illinois
La ley crea el Fondo de Apoyo a los Trabajadores de Vehículos Compartidos bajo la administración directa de la Secretaría de Estado de Illinois. Este fondo cubrirá de forma exclusiva los costos de implementación de la normativa y las subvenciones para la representación de los conductores.
Para sostener este sistema, las empresas de transporte abonarán una tasa obligatoria de cuatro centavos por cada viaje realizado en el estado. La legislación prohíbe de manera explícita que las plataformas cobren este monto adicional a los pasajeros.
En un comunicado, el secretario de Estado, Alexi Giannoulias, manifestó su total respaldo a la expansión de los derechos laborales en este sector moderno. El proceso de debate legislativo duró varios años y requirió múltiples audiencias en el Capitolio estatal en Springfield.

title: Việt Nam's new era needs talent with a passion to serve: Minister
content:
HÀ NỘI —Việt Nam is entering a new phase of development where science, technology, innovation, and high-quality human resources are increasingly becoming the decisive factors in national competitiveness. The country needs young people who are not only professionally skilled but also possess a profound desire to serve.
This was one of the core messages delivered by Minister of Science and Technology, Assoc. Prof. Dr. Vũ Hải Quân, to 126 outstanding students from 16 universities, along with 41 fellows and researchers from seven postgraduate institutes, during the Vallet Scholarship award ceremony held at the Temple of Literature in Hà Nội on Sunday.
The Odon Vallet Scholarship was established through the voluntary contributions of Dr. Odon Vallet, a Professor of Religious History at Sorbonne University, France. In Việt Nam, Professor Vallet entrusted the organisation of the scholarship programme to the "Rencontres du Vietnam" (Meeting Vietnam), co-founded and managed by Professor Trần Thanh Vân and his wife, Professor Lê Kim Ngọc.
Starting with 800 spots in 2001, the Odon Vallet Scholarship, to date, awarded approximately 55,000 scholarships with a total value exceeding VNĐ600 billion (approximately US$23 million). Recipients are not only excellent students from major cities but also those facing difficult circumstances from remote areas, mountainous regions, ethnic minority communities, and SOS Children's Villages across the country.
The value of each scholarship has also increased over time: university students and researchers now receive VNĐ34 million ($1,300) each, while high school students receive VNĐ17 million ($650). The award ceremony for high school students will take place on the morning of August 24 at the Âu Cơ Theater in Hà Nội.
“Professor Odon Vallet is a truly remarkable individual. He inherited a vast fortune, but his uniqueness lies not in the wealth itself, but in how he chose to use it,” said Minister Quân.
“Rather than spending it on his own life, he dedicated his resources to establishing scholarships for talented young people, starting in France, then expanding to Việt Nam and several other nations.”
“In Việt Nam, this story began with a meeting of two core convictions: the belief that knowledge can transform an individual's destiny, and the belief that investing in the youth is the ultimate investment in a nation's future," he added.
"If Odon Vallet offers us a story of generosity, Professor Trần Thanh Vân offers us a story of perseverance,” said Quân, recalling the fact that when Professor Vallet witnessed the educational missions of Rencontres du Vietnam, he proactively stepped in to contribute.
In 1993, Professor Vân returned to Việt Nam to organise the first 'Rencontres du Vietnam', bringing hundreds of world-renowned physicists, including Nobel laureates, to the country. From those scientific gatherings, a series of initiatives to train, connect, and support the young generation of Việt Nam took root.
Minister Quân said he found the name 'Rencontres du Vietnam' beautiful, “for science does not flourish in isolation. Science thrives on encounters: between individuals, between mentors and protégés, between Việt Nam and the world, and between ideas and opportunities. Professor Trần Thanh Vân has spent decades creating those very encounters.”
“From international conferences and physics schools to student workshops and scholarships, everything shares a single philosophy: identify talent, grant them opportunity, and help them surpass their own potential,” said the Minister of Science and Technology.
Speaking at the ceremony, Attaché for Scientific and Higher Education Cooperation at the French Embassy in Việt Nam, Denis Fourmeau, emphasised that “Education offers a wonderful perspective on the world, and science provides the fundamental tools to understand it. View these scholarships as an opportunity to bring your ideas to fruition. “
“Today's scientific challenges are complex: climate change, the preservation of biodiversity, healthcare, and the energies of tomorrow require a combination of creativity, rigor, and scientific excellence.
“To meet the challenges of our century, you will need, more than ever, to reach out and work together. Today's sciences are indeed multidisciplinary and global, and curiosity will be essential. Education may take you beyond the borders of Việt Nam, and your scientific curiosity beyond the frontiers of knowledge,” said Fourmeau.
Beyond the scholarships, 'Rencontres du Vietnam' also focuses on cultivating high-caliber talent. Starting in 2007, the association began selecting students who excelled in the National Math and Physics Olympiads to pursue their studies in France.
From 2009 to 2025, the Vietnam-France engineering programme has sent 246 students abroad, resulting in 206 engineering graduates and 18 PhDs. These efforts do more than just provide education; they open doors to global research for the younger generation and bridge the gap between science, education, and international partnership. VNS

title: Ulez led to better lung size and function among London children, study finds
content:
Children’s lungs grew bigger and stronger after the most polluting vehicles were restricted from entering London, a study has found.
Examinations of London schoolchildren before and after the introduction of the city’s ultra-low emission zone (Ulez) found a restoration of lung capacity that had been stunted by exposure to pollution.
The researchers said the findings were a vindication of the low-emission zone policy, which had been criticised as a burden on motorists.
“Traffic pollution in cities damages children’s health and development,” said Chris Griffiths, a professor of primary care at the University of Oxford and Queen Mary University of London (QMUL), and the study’s joint senior author.
“We provide the strongest evidence yet on how these harms can be prevented. Ambitious clean-air zones should be considered a priority for cities globally with traffic-related air pollution.”
Air pollution from traffic has stunted the development of children’s lungs in London for decades. Previous research found that by the age of eight or nine, children from the most polluted areas had 5-10% less lung capacity than their peers elsewhere.
That impairment, which scientists said was the result of exposure to nitrogen dioxide, put them at increased risk as adults of developing respiratory diseases, such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cardiovascular and metabolic disease, and premature death.
Londoners’ health was explicitly cited by the mayor, Sadiq Khan, to justify the introduction of Ulez – the world’s largest and most ambitious low-emission zone – in 2019. At the time, the policy, while intuitively sensible, lacked evidence, but researchers at QMUL saw an opportunity.
Before Ulez came into force, they recruited 1,664 children aged six to nine in London and 1,750 in Luton, which, as a town with a similar mix of traffic pollutants but no clean air zone, was used as a control.
The team measured and monitored the children’s size and health at annual school visits from 2018 to 2022 to assess how air quality changes after the introduction of Ulez had affected their lung development.
Initial measurements showed children in London had significantly smaller lungs compared with those in Luton. But after Ulez came into force, the size and health of the London children’s lungs improved until they were comparable with those of the children in Luton.
The children’s lung function improvements correlated strongly with air quality improvements. The researchers found that within five years of Ulez coming into force, the London children’s exposure to nitrogen dioxide fell twice as fast and twice as much as that of the Luton children.
Writing in the Guardian on Tuesday, Khan said: “Introducing and expanding the Ulez involved some incredibly difficult decisions. I never took them lightly, but I knew that – as mayor – I could not stand by while Londoners young and old lost their lives to a problem it was within my power to solve.
“For years, politicians and pundits opposed to the Ulez have cynically sought to turn questions of public health into a crude culture war. Today, though, it’s clear that we’re winning the battle against toxic air in the capital – and it’s London’s children who are reaping the rewards,” he added.
The health minister Karin Smyth said the study, published in the journal Lancet Public Health, was “a powerful reminder of the impact that air quality has on children’s lung health. “[It] will help to improve our understanding of how reductions in air pollution can restore normal lung growth among children, reduce the risk of respiratory illnesses in adulthood, and support our goal to give every child the best start in life.”
Stephen Burgess, a professor of biostatistics at the University of Cambridge who was not involved in the research, said it was not clear that the changes observed were truly attributable to Ulez, as opposed to other factors such as the impact of the Covid pandemic on pollution levels.
“Nevertheless, the finding is important because lung function in childhood is an important measure of health, and the study provides encouraging evidence that changes in the urban environment may benefit children’s lung development,” he said.

Cercanías estrena trenes en Madrid, Rodalies espera hacerlo a final de año
Movilidad
Los nuevos convoyes fabricados por Stadler empiezan a prestar servicio en la capital mientras los de Alstom siguen pendientes del permiso de seguridad ferroviaria
Los usuarios de Rodalies que vuelvan de las vacaciones se encontrarán las mismas limitaciones de velocidad y problemas en la red ferroviaria que había un mes antes. En cambio, el retorno a la rutina de los viajeros de Cercanías en Madrid va acompañado de novedades importantes, con nuevos trenes circulando por la capital española.
Esta semana se estrenan en la línea C7 las dos primeras unidades salidas de la fábrica de Stadler en Albuixech, una de 100 metros y otra de 200, ambas con vagones de dos pisos. Son convoyes con más pantallas de información y una capacidad un 20% superior, además de más puertas sin escalones –lo que agiliza la subida y bajada de pasajeros– y espacios para personas con movilidad reducida, bicicletas y carritos infantiles. A lo largo de los próximos meses se irán incorporando más trenes en el resto de las líneas del núcleo de Cercanías en Madrid hasta completar el pedido formado por 79 nuevas unidades.
El tren de Alstom para Rodalies está pendiente de la homologación de seguridad para poder entrar en servicio
En Catalunya habrá que esperar a finales de año, en el mejor de los casos. Los nuevos trenes de Rodalies no son del mismo fabricante, sino de Alstom y, en este caso, los plazos se han ido retrasando. Las pruebas de validación se vieron afectadas por la crisis de Rodalies a principios de año y por unos defectos en la fabricación que obligaron a hacer pequeños cambios en el diseño de los trenes, lo que le ha costado unas sonadas reprimendas públicas por parte del ministro de Transportes, Óscar Puente.
El pasado mes de mayo, con todo resuelto, la empresa fabricante entregó el dossier de homologación a la Agencia Española de Seguridad Ferroviaria (Aesf) y los dos primeros trenes preparados para circular salieron de la fábrica en junio. En las últimas semanas empiezan a acumularse las nuevas unidades en las vías de la planta de Alstom en el Vallès, de donde tendrán que salir por carretera, ya que las obras de la R3 impiden la utilización de la conexión ferroviaria.
El compromiso del fabricante francés es entregar antes de final de año las primeras 14 unidades del pedido de 201 trenes, de los cuales 72 se quedan en Catalunya y el resto irán al resto de España. También se esperan para mediados del año que viene nuevos trenes de CAF para los regionales.
La incorporación progresiva de los nuevos trenes supone una reorganización de la flota de Renfe. El primer movimiento son más de 40 trenes Civia de entre 14 y 23 años –con una larga vida por delante– que serán derivados de Madrid al núcleo de Cercanías de Valencia. Aunque supone un rejuvenecimiento de la flota, el traslado de trenes de “segunda mano” ha provocado una fuerte bronca entre el Ministerio de Transportes y el Gobierno valenciano.

title: Kod Mauritanije spašen 161 migrant na putu za Europu. "Ostali su bez vode i hrane"
content:
Kod Mauritanije spašen brod sa 161 migrantom. "Nestalo im je vode i hrane"
VLASTI Mauritanije, države na zapadu Afrike uz Atlantski ocean, objavile su danas da je obalna straža kod obale te zemlje presrela brod sa 161 migrantom na putu prema Europi. U priopćenju se navodi da su migranti spašeni u blizini ribarskog sela Amhijrat, sjeverno od glavnog grada Nouakchotta, piše AP.
Na brodu su bili državljani Senegala, Gvineje i Gambije, a među njima je bilo i 17 djece. Plovilo je isplovilo iz Banjula, glavnog grada Gambije, prije osam dana, a cilj putovanja bili su španjolski Kanarski otoci. Iz obalne straže potvrdili su da će sve osobe biti prebačene u prihvatni centar za migrante u Nouakchottu.
Iscrpljeni i bez hrane
Jedan imigracijski službenik, koji je htio ostati anoniman, izjavio je da su migranti zatečeni u teškom stanju. "Ostali su bez vode i hrane. Motor broda bio je potpuno dotrajao i neispravan, zbog čega se plovilo zaustavilo na otvorenom moru i više se nije moglo kretati", rekao je.
Mauritanske vode postale su jedna od glavnih ruta za stanovnike Afrike koji u Europi traže bolji život, potaknuti lošim ekonomskim prilikama u svojim zemljama. Prošlog mjeseca agencija UN-a za izbjeglice objavila je da je gotovo 150 ljudi poginulo ili nestalo s brodova kod Mauritanije.
Ruta prema Kanarskim otocima smatra se iznimno opasnom zbog velikih udaljenosti te nesigurnih i pretrpanih plovila. Prema podacima projekta "Missing Migrants" Međunarodne organizacije za migracije, tijekom 2025. na atlantskoj ruti od zapadne Afrike do Kanarskih otoka smrtno je stradalo najmanje 1200 migranata.

title: A multi-faceted hospital-based intervention for intrapartum care in sub-Saharan Africa: a stepped-wedge cluster-randomized trial
content:
Abstract
Around three million babies are stillborn or die shortly after birth each year worldwide, underscoring a persistent and unacceptable burden on families and health systems. To help address this challenge, we developed the facility-based, multi-faceted Action Leveraging Evidence to reduce perinatal Mortality and Morbidity (ALERT) intervention. ALERT promoted essential practices of intrapartum childbirth using (i) co-design, (ii) training, (iii) quality improvement and (iv) leadership mentoring. We evaluated ALERT using a stepped-wedge cluster-randomized trial with five 6-month periods across 16 hospitals in Benin, Malawi, Tanzania and Uganda. Among 134,630 women (including 139,300 neonates), the intervention was associated with 22% lower odds of the composite co-primary outcome, early perinatal mortality, defined as fresh stillbirth and 24 h neonatal mortality (adjusted odds ratio 0.78, 95% confidence interval 0.65–0.94), but not with the co-primary outcome, fresh stillbirth (adjusted odds ratio 0.88, 95% confidence interval 0.68–1.13). Despite the limitation of only including 16 hospitals, the diversity of settings across four sub-Saharan African countries supports the finding that early perinatal mortality and morbidity could be reduced through implementation of multi-faceted, context-specific strategies to build maternity provider capacities. Pan African Clinical Trial Registry: 202006793783148.
Similar content being viewed by others
Main
High maternal and perinatal mortality and morbidity rates prevail in sub-Saharan African countries (SSA)1,2,3. Nearly half of the global 1.9 million stillbirths and 2.3 million neonatal deaths annually occur in SSA, where both stillbirth and neonatal mortality rates remain above 20 per 1,000 births2. In addition, poorly managed labor and childbirth care leads to a large burden of morbidity, including cerebral palsy and neurological disorders caused by oxygen deprivation4,5,6.
Following the substantial increases in facility-based birth since the early 2000s, now exceeding 80% globally and over 60% in SSA today7,8, attention has shifted in recent years to the quality of pregnancy and childbirth care9,10. It is within this context that the World Health Organization (WHO) published a framework defining the quality of pregnancy and childbirth care in 201511 and recommendations for routine intrapartum care in 201812. This document complemented earlier guidance that focused on the management of the main maternal complications such as postpartum hemorrhage13, pre-eclampsia/eclampsia14, infection15 and preterm birth16. The later focus on the management of complications stimulated the development and evaluation of a large number of training programs17,18,19. For example, the Preterm Birth Initiative focused on an intervention package addressing specifically prematurity-related intra- and immediate postnatal care, including administration of corticosteroids, resuscitation and kangaroo care20. The Nepal quality improvement package equally focused on resuscitation as an important component of immediate postpartum care21. In contrast, no training program operationalizing the WHO 2018 intrapartum care guideline has been developed, beyond trials assessing distinct tools, such as the Safe Childbirth Checklist22 or the new WHO partograph23. Intrapartum care, however, is complex and demands a multitude of skills and decisions within multi-professional maternity care teams including readiness to apply the packages to address complications. The lack of attention to routine care, however, hinders programming for the Every Woman Every Newborn Everywhere (EWENE) global initiative, midwifery care models as well as more efficient management when complications occur24.
Guidelines and trainings are important steps towards improved care; however, achieving high-quality care requires a wider perspective. A variety of strategies have been proposed, spanning from certification and accreditation to quality assurance, collaborative quality improvement, and audit and feedback25,26,27. Reviews on what works to improve healthcare providers’ adherence to evidence-based guidelines have indicated that combinations of strategies including quality improvement strategies to build problem-solving competences show the greatest effects28,29,30. However, strategies with too many components are challenging to implement. The optimal combinations of implementation strategies addressing the complexity of intrapartum care considering implementability and scalability are yet to be defined. Furthermore, while co-design has been identified as an important strategy to shape contextually relevant solutions, the operationalization and value within quality improvement programs are unknown31.
The Action Leveraging Evidence to reduce perinatal Mortality and Morbidity in sub-Saharan Africa (ALERT) project addresses these two knowledge gaps and developed, implemented and evaluated a multi-faceted intervention to improve intrapartum care through a stepped-wedge cluster-randomized trial in 16 hospitals across 4 sub-Saharan African countries: Benin, Malawi, Tanzania and Uganda. The intervention was composed of (i) end-user participation of women, families and midwifery providers to co-design the intervention, (ii) in-service midwifery competency-based training, (iii) quality improvement, and (iv) empowerment and leadership mentoring of maternity unit leaders32 (Fig. 1). ALERT focused on proven evidence-based clinical interventions as well as the experience of care to improve the quality of care in a holistic manner and adapted to context. The intervention started with a co-design process which informed six training modules. The 3-day training sessions were supported by Laerdal Global Health MamaBirthie low-cost models33. Quality improvement used the Plan-Do-Study-Act cycles and promoted the documentation using quality improvement journals. Quarterly on-site mentoring and frequent phone calls with the maternity unit’s head supported the improvement work. The ALERT intervention targeted midwifery and clinical staff in the maternity wards of high-caseload hospitals34.
The main aim of this stepped-wedge cluster-randomized trial was to assess the effects of the ALERT intervention on the primary outcome of early perinatal mortality. We hypothesized that the intervention would reduce early perinatal mortality (stillbirths and neonatal deaths within 24 h) by 25% through synergistic action35. We assessed the intervention against standard care informed by national policies and characterized by resource constraints.
Results
Patient disposition
All 16 identified and randomized hospitals participated in the trial in line with the allocation produced and published on 17 June 2020 (Figs. 2 and 3, Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 1). We implemented five periods: 1 July to 31 December 2021 (baseline), 1 January to 30 June 2022, 1 July to 31 December 2022, 1 January to 30 June 2023 and 1 July to 31 December 2023. We included 134,630 women who gave birth to 139,300 neonates (July 2021 to December 2023) and 4,007 exit interviews to assess respectfulness and responsiveness. The stepped-wedge randomization design resulted in 60,403 births (45%) in comparison and 74,227 (55%) in intervention periods, showing a good balance across study arms and periods (Table 1 and Supplementary Table 2). Thirty percent of women were between 20 and 24 years old. Just under 40% were primipara. About a quarter (27.5% in the comparison and 22.8% in the intervention period) of the women arrived as referrals, 90% of whom were in active labor.
Intervention and reach
The intervention was initiated with competency-based in-facility training delivered to each hospital per country in accordance with the trial design and randomization, with slight delays (Figs. 2 and 3). Training was delivered as short, flexible sessions timed around shift changes with reinforcement sessions on subsequent days. A total of 484 maternity providers, quality improvement focal persons and administrative staff received the initial training, exceeding the 414 staff members originally registered as working in the trial hospitals owing to staff rotation demanding re-training36. A detailed fidelity assessment carried out in the final year of the trial showed that the ALERT team conducted 7, 12, 1 and 9 mentoring visits to hospitals in Benin, Malawi, Tanzania and Uganda, respectively. With the exception of Tanzania, the number of visits exceeded the six quarterly on-site mentoring visits specified in the protocol. A total of 112 h, 284h , 175h and 83 h of mentoring were delivered on-site and via WhatsApp in Benin, Malawi, Tanzania and Uganda, respectively, corresponding to an average of 56 h of mentoring per quarter per hospital.
Primary outcomes
Early (24 h) perinatal mortality decreased by 22% (adjusted odds ratio (OR) 0.78; 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.65–0.94) (Table 2 and Fig. 4). Fresh stillbirths showed a non-significant effect (adjusted OR 0.88; 95% CI 0.68–1.13).
Secondary outcomes
Hypoxic–ischemic events decreased by 19% in the intervention compared with the comparison period (adjusted OR 0.81; 95% CI 0.69–0.95). Further, we observed no significant effect on neonatal seizures (adjusted OR 0.79; 95% CI 0.55–1.15).
We observed a 14% increase in the odds of cesarean sections (adjusted OR 1.14; 95% CI 1.01–1.27), from 27.4% to 29.4% between comparison and intervention periods. We observed some associations with severe maternal morbidity (adjusted OR 0.83; 95% CI 0.61–1.13). Neither responsiveness nor respectful treatment (absence of mistreatment) scores changed significantly (coefficients 2.53 and −0.54, respectively) (Table 2 and Fig. 4).
Process outcomes
Process indicators, reflecting the intervention priorities, revealed that fetal heart monitoring on admission typically done using the Pinard stethoscope increased from 89% to 95% coverage (OR 25.05; 95% CI 9.20–68.23) (Table 2 and Supplementary Table 3). Documentation of ongoing fetal monitoring during labor improved (OR 2.05; 95% CI 1.11–3.79), while detection of fetal distress did not improve (OR 0.54; 95% CI 0.38–0.76) and neonatal resuscitation practices increased but not statistically significantly (OR 1.13; 95% CI 0.82–1.55).
We observed substantial heterogeneity between hospitals with I2 values exceeding 50% for most outcomes, supporting our decision to estimate hospital-specific effects before pooling results. Despite this variability, the direction of effect was broadly consistent: 13 of 16 hospitals showed reductions in early perinatal mortality, although individual estimates were often not statistically significant, reflecting limited power at the hospital level. However, distinct country-level patterns were seen. In Tanzania, early perinatal mortality rate declined from 15 to 9 per 1,000 births (hospitals 1 and 2), while hospital 3 showed an increase. In Uganda, hospital 2 saw a strong decline, while hospitals 1 and 4 had smaller gains while hospital 3 remained largely unchanged. Benin and Malawi showed more modest and variable improvements (Table 2 and Fig. 4).
Safety
Our adverse event monitoring as part of the process evaluation indicated no safety concerns in regard to the training and quality improvement. The 14% increase in the odds of cesarean sections was within expected ranges, supporting the safety of the intervention.
Post hoc analysis
Sensitivity, per-protocol analysis and temporal trends
We performed a sensitivity analysis excluding three hospitals following discussions of preliminary results with country teams in December 2024, which identified three hospitals (Tanzania Hospitals 3 and 4 and Malawi Hospital 3) as outliers owing to implementation barriers including limited staff engagement and data quality concerns. For example, hospital 3 in Malawi was a community hospital with severe resource constraints. Hospital 3 in Tanzania was part of another project where teams had to report during birth on process of labor, which we believe led to underreporting during the pre-intervention period and limited engagement in the trial because of fear of blame and disciplinary consequences. Details are found in the Supplementary Information (Extended Data Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 4). The analysis excluding these hospitals indicated results consistent with the main analysis. Per-protocol analysis was also consistent with the main analysis. The OR for fresh stillbirth was 0.86 (95% CI 0.67–1.10); for early perinatal mortality 0.77 (95% CI 0.64–0.91); hypoxic–ischemic events (OR 0.80; 95% CI 0.67–0.95) and cesarean section (OR 1.12; 95% CI 1.01–1.23) (Extended Data Fig. 3).
Three pre-specified sensitivity analyses requested during peer review (Hartung–Knapp–Sidik–Jonkman (HKSJ) pooling, per-protocol restricted to hospital-periods with documented full implementation, and country-stratified random-effects meta-analysis) gave results consistent with the primary analysis. For the primary outcome of early perinatal mortality, there was no evidence of between-country heterogeneity of effect (Qᵇ(3) = 1.61, P = 0.66). Full descriptions and outputs are provided in Supplementary Tables 5–7.
The primary intention-to-treat analysis retained all 16 hospitals. The three-hospital exclusion was post hoc, triggered by pre-specified data-quality monitoring indicators combined with structured contextual review with country teams in December 2024 (criteria in Supplementary Table 4).
Discussion
In this stepped-wedge cluster-randomized trial in 16 high-caseload hospitals in Benin, Malawi, Tanzania and Uganda, we developed, implemented and evaluated a multi-faceted intervention of co-design, training, quality improvement and mentorship. The intervention was associated with 22% lower odds of the composite outcome in-facility early perinatal mortality, 19% lower odds of hypoxic–ischemic events and a 14% increase in cesarean sections. Mortality reductions were likely underpinned by improved processes such as increased fetal heart rate monitoring and cesarean sections. We did not observe any effects on responsiveness or respectful care.
Our results suggesting 22% lower odds of in-facility early perinatal mortality concur with larger evaluations done in similar settings. The Preterm Birth Initiative in Kenya and Uganda reported 34% reduced odds of mortality in preterm neonates in response to a comprehensive quality improvement strategy20. Positive effects of interventions combining training, quality improvement and mentorship to improve intrapartum and early neonatal care are described by the Nepal Perinatal Quality Improvement study21,37,38, and the hospital initiative in the Democratic Republic of Congo39. Together, these findings reinforce the importance of multi-component strategies that address skills, systems and leadership simultaneously to achieve meaningful and sustained improvements in evidence-based practice and mortality, even if they are potentially resource intensive, as raised by others40. However, our economic analysis suggested limited costs of our approach41. For example, our co-design approach was not implemented in all hospitals and the mentoring approach relied largely on digital communication. In summary, our results support the importance of combining strategies to obtain greater changes in evidence-based practices and mortality28,42, while initiatives relying on quality improvement or training alone are increasingly recognized as insufficient to produce comparable mortality gains in resource-constrained settings20,43,44.
Our results also highlight the potential of routine intrapartum care as opposed to addressing emergency obstetric care as previous training and improvement packages have done17,18,19. Furthermore, our reduction in perinatal mortality and morbidity was achieved without technological innovations45. This highlights the potential effects of strengthening routine intrapartum care, that is, preventive and promotive midwifery care—an important finding towards the programming of the Every Woman Every Newborn Everywhere (EWENE) initiative24.
Our intervention adopted a health system strengthening lens targeting recurrent, cross-cutting challenges in intrapartum care46. Through co-design, the ALERT team and maternity care providers jointly identified key quality-of-care deficits, their underlying causes and how these were shaped by local healthcare constraints including providers’ competences and attitudes47. For example, co-design interviews with women postpartum highlighted that women missed important information on labor progress and why decisions were made48. Furthermore, hierarchical structures and power imbalances between women and providers led to breakdowns in communications49. These findings led to developing specific training components on communication and teamwork. We believe the co-design process created an empowering working relationship and traction for change (M.S., manuscript in preparation). The competency-based training reinforced essential intrapartum practices and translated co-designed solutions into routine clinical behaviors36.
We recognize that the positive effect on mortality was accompanied by an increase in cesarean section, which we interpret as a positive health systems strengthening effect. Population-based cesarean section rates in the included countries are at or below 10%, thus at levels where we would not expect an overuse of cesarean section50,51. Still, in low-resource hospital settings such as the ones in this study, cesarean section alone does not guarantee improved survival, particularly when delays in recognition or referral persist52,53. However, when considered alongside reductions in early perinatal mortality and hypoxic–ischemic events, the increase in cesarean section likely reflects more timely identification of complications and appropriate escalation of care. We therefore interpret this pattern as consistent with improved quality of intrapartum care rather than harmful overuse52.
Our intervention showed no effect on responsiveness or on respectful care, although the teams worked intensively to improve responsiveness, including companionship. Several possible reasons may explain this. First, we cannot exclude the possibility that our tools were not sensitive enough to capture change. Several studies have indicated that exit interviews before discharge are likely to underreport abuse and mistreatment, and this could have led to the fact that we could not report an effect54,55. Second, interpersonal skills, attitudes and behaviors might need more time before sustained changes can be expected. Third, policy and structural constraints made it difficult to introduce companionship56. Together, these factors may explain the absence of measurable effects on responsiveness and respectful care within the trial period.
The strength of this multi-country trial is the use of the stepped-wedge intervention design, a large number of births, and the inclusion of public and faith-based hospitals in four countries, improving generalizability. The use of the stepped-wedge trial design meant that all hospitals received the intervention, which enhanced engagement. Another strength was that while we adhered to structured processes, the outlined implementation strategy and a standardized curriculum, co-design, mentoring and quality improvement addressed local constraints in a flexible manner, thus arriving at a context-adapted, co-designed intervention with relevance to local context. We kickstarted our intervention using co-design methodologies, which allowed providers to influence the intervention and targeted routine intrapartum care, underscoring the potential of improving basic childbirth and preventive midwifery care as opposed to specifically addressing selected emergency obstetric conditions45,57.
Our analytical approach had several strengths. First, we used hospital-specific mixed-effects models, rather than a single pooled analysis, acknowledging heterogeneity, confirmed by I2 values exceeding 50%. This avoided the ecological fallacy of assuming uniform intervention effects across settings. Second, the random-effects meta-analysis preserved this heterogeneity while providing overall estimates. Forest plots transparently displayed both individual hospital effects and uncertainty. Third, the intention-to-treat framework maintained the benefits of randomization, while sensitivity analyses (excluding sites with data quality concerns and per-protocol analysis) tested the robustness of our findings. Fourth, we had minimal missing data, reducing selection bias.
Our study faces limitations, one of which was the start of our trial in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic, which precluded face-to-face meetings during the critical co-design and start-up period. The trial started with a 6-month delay, limiting the financial space. One consequence was that we were unable to introduce the lactate testing in a sub-sample.
Our two primary and four of six secondary outcomes were assessed using an innovative e-registry data collection tool supported by rigorous quality assurance. Still, we cannot fully exclude underreporting of perinatal events, which is why we included a sensitivity analysis. National accountability measures, as applied in Tanzania, disincentivized maternity providers from reporting deaths for fear of repercussions58. Furthermore, we were not able to follow up neonates for longer than 24 h after childbirth, thus beyond discharge, to establish neonatal mortality. While we achieved extremely low missing data (1,000 g between 1 July 2021 and 31 December 2023 in an intention-to-treat analysis66. We expanded the inclusion period in Benin, Malawi and Tanzania to February 2024 because of implementation delays in our per-protocol analysis (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Information 9, Statistical Analysis Plan). We excluded mother-baby pairs that arrived at the hospitals after giving birth, unless one of multiples was born in the participating hospital.
Intervention
The ALERT intervention focused on the quality of intrapartum care targeting maternity providers in the included hospitals. We developed the intervention using a co-design process complemented by facility and knowledge assessments48,49,67 (January and September 2021) (Fig. 1). Training materials were developed addressing knowledge deficits and implementation challenges17,68. The implementation started with a 3-day training33, during which locally prioritized improvement topics were selected. Subsequently, maternity teams implemented and evaluated improvements under mentorship from ALERT researchers. The focus on mortality and experience of care was thought to be complementary. Responsiveness offers an opportunity to adapt care to changing women’s needs, promote women’s access to effective interventions and improve the quality of services34.
Outcomes
The trial’s primary outcomes were in-facility (fresh) stillbirths defined as the number of fresh stillbirths of at least 1,000 g per 1,000 live- and stillbirths and a composite early perinatal mortality indicator defined as in-facility (fresh) stillbirths and 24 h neonatal mortality defined as death of a neonate within 24 h after birth per 1,000 live- and stillbirths, both assessed using our perinatal e-registry32. Secondary outcomes were hypoxic–ischemic events defined as a neonate with Apgar <7 at 5 min, neonatal seizures, cesarean sections, severe maternal morbidities defined as women with hysterectomy, laparotomy, blood transfusion, admission to an intensive care unit or referral to a higher-level facility, all expressed per 1,000 live- and stillbirths using the perinatal e-registry. Our respectful-care-focused secondary outcomes were responsiveness and respectful treatment (1 minus mistreatment). They were assessed using exit interviews with women after having given birth. Process measures were not pre-specified owing to the co-design of the intervention leading to adapted training and intervention components in the development phase. We report on fetal heart rate check at admission, fetal monitoring during the first stage of labor, detection of fetal distress, resuscitation of babies, companionship and breastfeeding within 1 h of birth. Details of the process indicators are listed in Supplementary Table 8. Cost-effectiveness and implementation process findings will be reported elsewhere35.
Sample size
We used a sample size formula for stepped-wedge trials32,69. The study was sufficiently powered (75–80%) to detect a 25% reduction in the outcome perinatal mortality with baseline rates between 1.4% and 2.0% and a 30% reduction in intrapartum stillbirth assuming a baseline rate of 1% and 95% CIs. Details are available in the supplementary file of the protocol32.
Data collection
Data from patient files, birth registers and case notes were entered in a preprogrammed e-registry application in the Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) platform59. Data collectors underwent a 2-day training in March 2021, after which a 4-month pilot data collection phase started. Each tablet had a personalized token and password; data were uploaded daily. Data quality assurance included (1) automated data validation and logical checks in REDCap, (2) bi-weekly audits by running pre-prepared Stata do-files, and (3) cross-checking of entries against paper records.
To assess experience of care, we conducted exit interviews using a questionnaire adapted from established responsiveness and mistreatment questionnaires70,71. We performed an exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis, which identified six factors: ‘Communication & supportive care’, ‘Hospital environment’, ‘Maintained respect & dignity’, ‘Social support’, ‘Maintained privacy & confidentiality’ and ‘Lack of physical & verbal abuse’. Findings were summarized in two summative scores to construct a responsiveness and respectful care (1 minus mistreatment) score72. In line with the stepped-wedge trial, we included a sample of 50 women per hospital recruited into the perinatal e-registry at five time periods. Data collectors applied a randomization factor to recruit the target number in each hospital based on the number of eligible women being discharged from the study hospitals73.
Selection of hospitals and randomization
Hospitals were purposively selected in March 2020, drawing from a national facility list to identify high-caseload hospitals. Criteria included (i) minimum caseload of 2,500 births per year; (ii) availability of cesarean section and blood transfusion; (iii) preferably located in rural districts; (iv) consisting of a mix of typical public and (faith-based) hospitals; and (v) interest in collaboration and no other ongoing initiative focusing on intrapartum care32. The final selection was done in consultation with the Ministry of Health and took into account feasibility concerns in terms of travel time between the hospitals to ensure operational efficiency.
Randomization using Stata and a pre-prepared code was carried out on 17 June 2020 by an independent statistician after obtaining consent from the participating hospitals (Supplementary Information Statistical Analysis Plan). Stratification by country was used to enable random allocation of the four hospitals. Maternity providers were not blinded to the intervention, and women and their families receiving care at these hospitals were aware of the quality improvement intervention.
Safety monitoring
Safety oversight was provided by the independent Data Safety Monitoring Board. The preliminary Statistical Analysis Plan stated the development of clear stopping rules at approximately 50% and 75% of the planned sample size using pre-specified stopping criteria. However, in consultation with the Data Safety Monitoring Board, we agreed that clear stopping rules are difficult to apply for a non-clinical intervention such as training and quality improvement, which is universally perceived as valuable.
We monitored the safety of our approach by analyzing and discussing changes in the cesarean section rates during meetings with our Data and Safety Monitoring Board. Our main outcomes were maternal and neonatal events constituting safety measures. In addition, we monitored, as part of our process evaluation, any severe events happening in the hospitals such as disruptions owing to climate or political events, staff rotation, interruptions in supplies, allegations owing to severe events in the maternity and similar. Our team followed a debriefing protocol where such events were discussed within the ALERT team to support the mentors in acting appropriately.
Statistical analysis
We used an intention-to-treat approach, analyzing all data at woman- and baby-level within the 16 hospitals according to their assigned intervention status. The 30-month study period was divided into 5 discrete 6-month intervals (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Information 9, Statistical Analysis Plan).
Descriptive analyses using frequencies and percentages for categorical variables, and median and interquartile ranges for continuous variables were conducted. Hospital-specific mixed-effects regression models were fitted to account for heterogeneity. We first considered generalized estimating equations adjusting for clusters and for the small sample32. However, in view of the heterogeneity, this statistical approach was not implementable.
Two primary outcomes were pre-specified. No formal adjustment for multiplicity was planned or applied because both outcomes were considered clinically important and the analyses followed the pre-specified statistical analysis plan. The two outcomes are closely related, with fresh stillbirth forming part of the composite perinatal mortality outcome.
For binary outcomes (primary and composite outcome) as well as the binary secondary outcomes, we used logistic mixed-effects models with random intercepts for intervention periods and presented ORs (95% CI). For continuous outcomes (responsiveness and respectful treatment scores), we used linear mixed-effects models and presented mean differences (95% CI). To account for time period effects and the stepped-wedge design structure, all models included the treatment status (intervention versus comparison) and time period (6-month intervals). Random intercepts were used for sequential randomization groups to account for clustering.
Hospital-specific effects were subsequently pooled using random-effects meta-analysis with the DerSimonian–Laird method and displayed as forest plots. Heterogeneity was assessed using I2 statistics, with values above 50% indicating substantial heterogeneity. We conducted sensitivity analyses by excluding hospitals identified as outliers based on both statistical and contextual considerations. Following discussions of preliminary results with country teams in December 2024, three hospitals (Tanzania Hospitals 3 and 4 and Malawi Hospital 3) were identified as outliers owing to fundamental implementation barriers, including lack of fetal monitoring capacity, data quality and limited staff engagement (Supplementary Table 4).
Per-protocol analysis
We also conducted a per-protocol analysis using an alternative definition of the intervention period to ensure full implementation fidelity (Extended Data Fig. 3). Secondary outcomes and process indicators are presented without adjustment for multiple testing, as pre-specified in the Statistical Analysis Plan; they should be interpreted on consistency of direction and magnitude rather than on individual P values.
Temporal trends
Temporal trends over time across all facilities were examined for primary and select secondary outcomes (Extended Data Fig. 4). As missing data for the primary outcomes were minimal (<1%), complete case analysis was done. Statistical analyses were performed using Stata Standard Edition 18.
Sensitivity analyses
In response to peer review, three pre-specified sensitivity analyses were additionally performed (HKSJ pooling, per-protocol re-analysis and country-stratified random-effects pool); full methodological detail and results are provided in Supplementary Methods and Supplementary Tables 5–7.
Hartung–Knapp–Sidik–Jonkman pooling
Because the number of clusters is small (k = 15–16), we re-pooled the hospital-specific estimates using the HKSJ method, which combines a restricted-maximum-likelihood estimate of between-hospital variance with a t-distribution on k − 1 degrees of freedom. Point estimates were essentially unchanged from the DerSimonian–Laird pool used in the main analysis, and CIs were slightly wider (Supplementary Table 6).
Per-protocol analysis considering quality concerns
Three hospitals (Tanzania Hospitals 3 and 4 and Malawi Hospital 3) were prospectively identified as unable to deliver the intervention package, following country-team review meetings in December 2024 and before the analytical code was locked. Three criteria, agreed in advance, were applied: (i) documented absence of core intervention components (for example, Malawi Hospital 3 had no functional fetal monitoring equipment); (ii) implementation barriers recorded in site-level process-evaluation notes, such as low staff engagement and concerns about data fidelity at Tanzania Hospital 3 following an external audit, and low case volume with incomplete outcome data at Tanzania Hospital 4; and (iii) hospital-period cells in which the full package was not delivered, captured by the trial’s ‘perprotocol’ indicator. The hospitals meeting these criteria are listed in Supplementary Table 4. The pool was restricted to hospital-periods with ‘perprotocol = 1’. Point estimates attenuated for most outcomes, but their direction was unchanged; between-hospital heterogeneity (I2) fell substantially (Supplementary Table 7).
Country-stratified pooling
The 16 hospital-specific estimates were pooled within each country, and a between-country Q-test with 3 degrees of freedom was used to test for heterogeneity of treatment effect across Benin, Malawi, Tanzania and Uganda. For the primary outcome of early perinatal mortality, there was no evidence of between-country heterogeneity (Qᵇ(3) = 1.61, P = 0.66). For fresh stillbirth, cesarean section, severe maternal morbidity, fetal distress and breastfeeding within 1 h, between-country heterogeneity was significant (P < 0.05) (Supplementary Table 7).
Protocol deviations
We were not able to implement lactate testing as a measure independent of clinical judgment to indicate hypoxic–ischemic events for operational and financial reasons. However, we included lactate testing using the Nova lactate point-of-care meter for 437 cases of Apgar <7 in 2 hospitals in Uganda. A total of 420 of 437 (96%) neonates born with an Apgar <7 had a lactate level above 5.5 mmol l−1, confirming earlier work indicating reasonable sensitivity and specificity of the Apgar score in this setting52,74. We were unable to construct the process indicator decision-to-birth time for cesarean section because the team did not document this consistently.

Data availability
Data from the perinatal e-registry will be made available from 31 December 2027, which is 3 years following the finalization of the trial, in accordance with the ALERT data management plan and publication policy. This restriction was instituted to allow country researchers from Benin, Malawi, Tanzania and Uganda, particularly early-career researchers and PhD students, time to conduct analyses and publish findings. Before this date, data can be made available after consideration by the ALERT steering committee, which is led by the corresponding author, C. H.
The ALERT data dictionary and supporting documents are available at https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/847824/results. Researchers from any country with an affiliation to a recognized university or research institution are eligible to apply for access to the ALERT dataset, and applicants should submit a detailed project proposal (no more than five pages) to the corresponding author, outlining the project aims, methodology, requested variables, planned statistical analyses, evidence of ethics approval and benefit to local countries. The criteria used to evaluate the requests are (i) scientific merit, (ii) feasibility, (iii) benefit for local countries and (iv) ethical considerations. The ALERT steering committee will respond to all data requests within 1 month and, if approved, the data will be released shortly after approval. Access to data may be restricted if members of the ALERT team are planning or conducting similar analyses.

title: Experts: Illicit alcohol crackdown should go beyond enforcement
content: The recent crackdown and recall of illicit alcohol products could contribute to efforts to improve mental health among vulnerable communities, mental health practitioners have said. However, they noted that enforcement should be accompanied by prevention, public education, psychosocial support and services for people struggling with substance use. ALSO READ: The fight against illicit alcohol is for our future They made the comments this week in Kigali during an event organised by the National Union of Disability Organisations of Rwanda (NUDOR) and Impanuro Girls Initiative to equip trainers with stress-management skills that they will later pass on to vulnerable communities. Emile Cadet Vuningabo, Head of Programmes at NUDOR, said reducing access to harmful products could help address some factors linked to mental health and sexual and reproductive health challenges. ALSO READ: Autism and mental health: A growing public health priority for Rwanda and Africa “Alcohol misuse can increase vulnerability to mental health challenges and can also contribute to risky sexual behaviour, gender-based violence and sexual violence,” he said. Dr Chaste Uwihoreye, a mental health lecturer, said Ministry of Health data shows that 18 per cent of Rwandans have at least one symptom of a mental health problem. “Drug and alcohol use are among the main drivers of mental health problems,” he said, adding that research conducted in 2018 found that 12 per cent of Rwandans experienced stress. He said the training-of-trainers approach would help extend support to vulnerable communities. “The crackdown on illicit alcohol will contribute a lot to mental health promotion. You cannot keep someone to dry while they are standing in the rain; similarly, it is difficult to protect someone's mental health while they continue using harmful substances,” he said. Nawali Nsengiyumva, Acting Executive Director of Impanuro Girls Initiative, said many young people they work with have experienced difficult situations that cause them to withdraw from others. She said the trainers would help young people develop ways of dealing with stress arising from different challenges, including disability and HIV. “We want the young people we serve to heal and, in turn, empower their communities,” she said.

title: Expert Explains | India-China boundary talks: Some progress, but a long road ahead
content:
5 min readNew DelhiAug 28, 2026 06:58 PM IST
First published on: Aug 28, 2026 at 07:00 AM IST



The eight-point consensus reached at the 25th round of talks between Special Representatives (SRs) Ajit Doval and his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi in Beijing is a welcome step ahead of the expected visit of President Xi Jinping to India for the BRICS Summit.
Some of the outcomes concern the maintenance of peace and tranquillity in the border areas, and advancing negotiations on a framework for the settlement of the boundary question in accordance with previous agreements. There is a specific reference to advancing discussions through an Expert Group and Working Group respectively, to explore an “early harvest” of boundary delimitation in appropriate sectors, and effective border management.
Last year, there was agreement in principle on working towards setting up additional General-Level Mechanisms/Senior Highest Military Commander (SHMC) meetings in the Eastern and Middle sectors akin to the existing mechanism in the Western sector at Chushul/Moldo.
This time, the two sides agreed to implement that understanding along with establishing two hotlines in the Eastern and Middle Sectors. Going forward, the implementation will have to be handled carefully.
National Security Advisor (NSA) Ajit Doval with China Foreign Affairs Minister Wang Yi ahead of the 25th round of Special Representatives (SR), in Beijing, China. (Handout via PTI Photo)
The past as prologue
In 1992, the Joint Working Group (JWG) on the Boundary Question decided on confidence building measures (CBMs) such as border personnel meetings (BPMs), complementing forward movement on border trade.
A sub-group of the JWG was created following the border peace and tranquillity agreement (BPTA) of 1993 — the India-China Expert Group of Diplomatic and Military Officials (EG), a precursor to the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on India-China Border Affairs (WMCC), an institutional mechanism for border management set up in 2012.
After the success achieved in 1995 on disengagement at Sumdorong Chu (along the India-China Line of Actual Control in Arunachal Pradesh), Lipulekh (Middle Sector) and Dichu (Eastern Sector) were subsequently identified as additional military meeting points. The plan for BPMs at Lipulekh was abandoned due to lack of infrastructure and adverse weather conditions. A trial meeting at Dichu in the Kibithu sector in Arunachal Pradesh was finalised. Dichu is a sensitive area in Anjaw district, and the site of a famous battle in 1962 at Hill 100, in which the Kumaon Regiment did the Indian Army proud. The site chosen for the BPM on Madan Ridge proved contentious. No further meetings could take place.
It was not until 2014 that the proposal for additional points for BPMs was revived. Eventually, it was decided to have regular BPMs at Wacha/Kibithu in the same sector opposite Damai on the Chinese side, in addition to existing venues across Bum La in Arunachal Pradesh and Nathu La in Sikkim.
Together with BPMs across the Lungnak Lungpa stream at Daulat Beg Oldie (DBO) and Tianwendian (TWD) in the Chip Chap valley, and at the Chushul–Moldo meeting point in the Spanggur Gap, these have contributed to the two militaries maintaining direct contact.
Additional meetings would further the cause of peace.
Existing hotlines at DBO and Chushul, some informal communication at Demchok in the Western Sector, and similar hotlines at Nathu La (Sikkim) and Bum La and Kibithu in the Eastern Sector have provided the two militaries with channels for direct contact. The two additional hotline channels agreed to for the Eastern and Middle sectors could strengthen this capacity and help defuse local tensions.
The road ahead
The SRs are working to realise the consensus reached between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Xi at Kazan in October 2024 and at Tianjin in August 2025 on improving ties.
Recent developments such as the resumption of the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra, direct flights, and border trade are meaningful steps in the right direction.
However, the road ahead, especially on the task of “early and substantial harvest of boundary delimitation and border management” may be long and arduous, requiring patient negotiations. It would be premature to suggest that substantive boundary delimitation has already begun in earnest. After all, the Expert Group and Working Group under the WMCC are now explicitly tasked with finalising their respective Terms of Reference. That means the framework is being created and the process is being activated incrementally.
There is also the issue of making piecemeal progress as against a more holistic settlement of differences along the Line of Actual Control. Neither the Sikkim sub-sector nor the Middle Sector are free from the burden of differences. The negotiators must be empowered to engage in meaningful discussions. They must have sufficient experience in handling a matter that has proved vexatious for previous generations.
If taken in the right direction, the guidance provided by the political leadership can lead to lasting peace and offer a window for substantive cooperation between two large and populous neighbours in an era of global flux.
(The author is Director General, Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses. He was also head of the Indian side in the Expert Group of Diplomatic and Military Officials negotiating with China between 1996 and 2000)

title: Zambia’s carbon registry could mark a turning point for Africa’s carbon market
content:
In January 2026, one of Africa’s most ambitious clean cooking companies shut down operations. KOKO Networks had raised over $100 million and was backed by a $180 million World Bank guarantee designed to shield investors from losses caused by government actions. It had reached more than 1.5 million households across Kenya with a clean cooking business built to displace charcoal.
KOKO had built the business. What it could not secure was the Kenyan government’s approval to sell the carbon credits its business model depended on. The Letter of Authorisation that Article 6 of the Paris Agreement requires never arrived, and the revenue that would have funded KOKO’s subsidies disappeared with it.
A carbon credit is, in plain terms, a tradeable certificate. Each one certifies that somewhere in Africa, a tonne of carbon dioxide (CO₂) that would have entered the atmosphere did not, because a forest was protected, a cleaner stove replaced a dirtier one, or a solar plant displaced a diesel generator.
Governments and companies buy them to offset emissions they cannot yet eliminate, either to meet regulatory obligations or to satisfy net-zero commitments made to investors and customers. A credit’s price and legitimacy depend on whether the reduction is real, additional, permanent, and, critically, counted only once. That last requirement is why national registries exist.
On August 11, 2026, the Government of Zambia launched a fully operational national carbon registry, becoming the second African country after Ghana to combine live registry infrastructure with a signed bilateral agreement and a completed transaction. That combination now exists in two African markets.
What a registry actually does, and why it matters
To understand why Zambia’s launch is consequential, it helps to understand what a national registry actually does. Article 6 of the Paris Agreement allows countries to trade emissions reductions internationally, but only if those reductions are formally authorised, tracked, and adjusted in the host country’s national accounting so they cannot be counted twice.
A national registry is the digital infrastructure that makes all of this possible. Without one, a project developer can generate perfectly legitimate carbon credits and still be unable to sell them, because there is no institutional mechanism to authorise the transaction. That is precisely the gap KOKO fell through, and it is precisely the gap Zambia has just closed.
The registry is already anchored by a live transaction.
In January 2026, Zambia signed a Mitigation Outcome Purchase Agreement with Norway under the Carbon Feed-in Premium programme, a mechanism designed to trigger up to 300 megawatts of new solar and battery storage capacity in Zambia and reduce up to 3.5 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent over a decade.
The same programme is now drawing local and international power developers into a business model where every tonne of carbon they help avoid is bought by the Norwegian government at a pre-agreed price. That combination, a signed agreement between two governments, a working national registry to track the credits, and a pipeline of developers ready to build, is what Ghana pioneered and Zambia has now replicated.
For a Zambian solar developer, it means a second, guaranteed revenue stream on top of the electricity they sell, one predictable enough that a bank can lend against it. For Norway, it means credits that will hold up under scrutiny.
The private-sector pipeline extends beyond solar. BioCarbon Partners has been running the 1.2-million-hectare Luangwa Community Forests Project since 2014. Pro Green Earth is developing the Barotse Rangelands Restoration Project across an additional 1.2 million hectares in Western Province, with validation of the project design document expected this year. Between them, forestry and rangelands account for more than 2.4 million hectares under active carbon project development.
The continental picture is evolving
Zambia is not moving alone, and this is where the market is being repriced. Ghana has signed at least ten Article 6 cooperation agreements in 2026 and operates a live Ghana Carbon Registry under its Environmental Protection Act 2025, and in July 2025 completed the first-ever ITMO transfer in Africa; nearly 12,000 verified units moved to Switzerland under their bilateral agreement. Access Bank Ghana was authorised as a carbon-credit broker in August 2026, an early sign that a financial intermediation layer is forming around the market. Eight southern African countries launched a regional carbon market alliance in April. In West Africa, ECOWAS is validating a regional framework designed to close a $294 billion climate finance gap. What has been a fragmented policy ambition for a decade is beginning to consolidate into functional market infrastructure.
The scale of what this unlocks is significant. The Africa Carbon Markets Initiative projects the continent’s carbon market could scale roughly nineteen-fold by 2030, generating around $6 billion in annual revenue and supporting up to 30 million jobs. Some industry sources project that the market could exceed $50 billion in high-demand scenarios driven by compliance with the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) and tightening corporate net-zero commitments. Whether the market reaches the lower or upper end of that range depends almost entirely on whether the institutional infrastructure Zambia has just launched becomes the norm rather than the exception across the continent.
What still has to go right
An operational registry is a precondition for transactions, not a guarantee of them. Four risks sit between the architecture Zambia has built and the market it hopes to convene.
Macroeconomic risk is the first. Zambia defaulted on its sovereign debt in 2020 and completed restructuring only in 2024. Buyers underwriting ten-year credit streams denominated in a volatile kwacha will price that in. Government-to-government agreements with Norway and Sweden partially cushion this; private developers raising commercial finance will not.
Demand-side risk is the second. The Article 6 market is unproven at a commercial scale. The first-ever credit issuance under the new Article 6.4 mechanism was approved in February 2026 for a single clean-cooking project in Myanmar, and as of mid-2026, only 13% of legacy CDM credits requesting transition had been approved. Whether corporate buyers will pay the prices needed to make African projects bankable remains an open question.
Domestic equity is the third. Zambia has a track record of community benefit-sharing disputes in existing REDD+ projects; how carbon revenues reach the chiefdoms whose forests generate them has stalled projects across the continent. The Green Economy and Climate Change Act of 2024 sets rules for benefit-sharing but has not been tested on a large-scale Article 6 transaction under commercial pressure.
Time is the fourth. The registry is now live, but the pipeline it processes has its own clock. The Miombo Woodland Restoration project is not scheduled to issue credits until 2027, and the Carbon Feed-in Premium programme, which closed applications in May 2026, will take months to move from award to verified reductions.
Taken together, these risks do not undo Zambia’s progress. They define what it actually is. Zambia has not fixed Africa’s carbon market. What it has done is become the second jurisdiction where the model can be tested at a commercial scale.
What it means and who benefits
For project developers building on carbon revenue models, the era of hoping for authorisation is ending. The African markets that will attract capital and buyers in the next 18 months are the ones that can point to an operational registry, a signed bilateral agreement, and a completed first transaction. Ghana and Zambia now have all three.
For investors and development finance institutions, the question is shifting from which African countries have carbon market potential to which African countries can actually transact. Capital that could be spread across the continent will begin to concentrate in jurisdictions that have crossed the transaction-readiness threshold.
For African policymakers, Ghana and Zambia together provide a working template. The Green Economy and Climate Change Act of 2024, the operational registry, the Norway agreement, and the pipeline of Article 6 projects together form a playbook that other governments can adapt. The countries that move fastest to replicate this architecture will likely attract projects, capital, and credit demand. Africa’s carbon market is entering its transaction phase.
